title: Percentages
subtitle: Quantitative Aptitude – Placement Preparation
description: Learn percentage fundamentals, important formulas, shortcuts and common placement-question patterns.
learningObjectives: Convert fractions and decimals into percentages.
Find a percentage of a quantity.
Solve marks, salary, population, expenditure and election problems.
Apply percentage shortcuts in placement assessments.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning of Percentage
content: The word percentage means per hundred.
A percentage represents a number or quantity as a fraction of 100.
The symbol used for percentage is %.
For example, 35% means 35 out of every 100.
formulas: Percentage = (Part / Whole) × 100

examples.question: Express 25% as a fraction.
A student answered 36 questions correctly out of 40. Find the percentage.

sections.heading: 2. Converting Fractions into Percentages
content: To convert a fraction into a percentage, multiply the fraction by 100.
Memorising common fraction-percentage values improves speed in aptitude assessments.
formulas: Percentage = Fraction × 100

examples.question: Convert 3/5 into a percentage.
Convert 7/8 into a percentage.

sections.heading: 3. Converting Decimals into Percentages
content: To convert a decimal into a percentage, multiply the decimal by 100.
Move the decimal point two places to the right and add the percentage symbol.
formulas: Percentage = Decimal × 100

examples.question: Convert 0.65 into a percentage.
Convert 1.25 into a percentage.

sections.heading: 4. Converting Percentages into Fractions or Decimals
content: To convert a percentage into a fraction, divide it by 100 and simplify.
To convert a percentage into a decimal, divide it by 100.
formulas: Fraction = Percentage / 100
Decimal = Percentage / 100

examples.question: Convert 45% into a fraction.
Convert 72% into a decimal.

sections.heading: 5. Finding a Percentage of a Quantity
content: Replace the percentage symbol with division by 100 and multiply by the given quantity.
The word of usually indicates multiplication.
formulas: x% of y = (x/100) × y
x% of y = y% of x

examples.question: Find 20% of 450.
Find 25% of 360.
Find 8% of 50.

sections.heading: 6. Finding the Whole when a Percentage is Given
content: Sometimes a percentage value is given and the original total must be found.
Represent the total as 100% and use direct proportion.
formulas: Whole = (Given value × 100) / Given percentage

examples.question: 30% of a number is 72. Find the number.
A student scored 360 marks, which is 80% of the total. Find the total marks.

sections.heading: 7. Percentage Increase
content: Percentage increase measures how much a value has increased compared with its original value.
Always divide the increase by the original value, not by the new value.
formulas: Increase = New value − Original value
Percentage increase = (Increase / Original value) × 100
New value after r% increase = Original value × (100 + r) / 100

examples.question: A value increases from 200 to 250. Find the percentage increase.
A salary of 40,000 increases by 15%. Find the new salary.

sections.heading: 8. Percentage Decrease
content: Percentage decrease measures how much a value has fallen compared with its original value.
The original value is always the denominator.
formulas: Decrease = Original value − New value
Percentage decrease = (Decrease / Original value) × 100
New value after r% decrease = Original value × (100 − r) / 100

examples.question: A price decreases from 500 to 425. Find the percentage decrease.
A machine worth 80,000 depreciates by 10%. Find its new value.

sections.heading: 9. Successive Percentage Changes
content: When a quantity changes more than once, do not simply add or subtract the percentages.
Each new percentage is applied to the changed value.
The net-change shortcut is useful when two successive changes are given.
formulas: Net percentage change = a + b + (a × b)/100
Use a positive sign for an increase.
Use a negative sign for a decrease.

examples.question: A value increases by 20% and then increases by 10%. Find the net percentage change.
A price increases by 20% and then decreases by 20%. Find the net change.
examples.solution: Net change = 20 − 20 + (20 × −20)/100 = −4%. Therefore, there is a 4% decrease.

examples.question: A population decreases by 10% and then increases by 10%. Find the net change.
examples.solution: Net change = −10 + 10 + (−10 × 10)/100 = −1%. Therefore, there is a 1% decrease.

sections.heading: 10. Restoring a Value after an Increase or Decrease
content: Equal percentage increase and decrease do not cancel each other.
A different percentage is needed to return to the original value.
formulas: Required decrease after an r% increase = [r / (100 + r)] × 100
Required increase after an r% decrease = [r / (100 − r)] × 100

examples.question: A price is increased by 25%. By what percentage must it be reduced to return to the original price?
A value decreases by 20%. By what percentage must it increase to return to its original value?

sections.heading: 11. Comparing Two Quantities
content: When comparing A with B, the reference quantity is important.
If A is greater than B, divide the difference by B.
If A is less than B, divide the difference by B.
formulas: A is what percent more than B = [(A − B) / B] × 100
A is what percent less than B = [(B − A) / B] × 100

examples.question: A is 150 and B is 120. A is what percent more than B?
A is 80 and B is 100. A is what percent less than B?

sections.heading: 12. More-Than and Less-Than Relationship
content: If A is r% more than B, B is not r% less than A.
The percentage changes because the reference quantity changes.
formulas: If A is r% more than B, B is [r / (100 + r)] × 100% less than A.
If A is r% less than B, B is [r / (100 − r)] × 100% more than A.

examples.question: A is 25% more than B. B is what percent less than A?
A is 20% less than B. B is what percent more than A?

sections.heading: 13. Marks and Examination Problems
content: Marks questions commonly involve pass percentage, failure margin, maximum marks or difference between two students.
Convert the percentage into marks using the total maximum marks.
formulas: Marks obtained = (Percentage / 100) × Maximum marks
Percentage scored = (Marks obtained / Maximum marks) × 100

examples.question: A student scores 72% of 500 marks. Find the marks obtained.
The pass mark is 40%. A student scores 168 marks and fails by 32 marks. Find the maximum marks.
examples.solution: Pass marks = 168 + 32 = 200. Since 200 is 40%, maximum marks = (200 × 100)/40 = 500.

sections.heading: 14. Income, Expenditure and Savings
content: Savings are calculated by subtracting expenditure from income.
When expenditure is given as a percentage of income, the remaining percentage represents savings.
formulas: Savings = Income − Expenditure
Savings percentage = 100% − Expenditure percentage

examples.question: A person spends 75% of their income. What percentage is saved?
A person earns 50,000 and saves 20%. Find the expenditure.

sections.heading: 15. Population Growth and Depreciation
content: Repeated population growth and depreciation are applications of compound percentage change.
The percentage is applied to the value at the beginning of each period.
formulas: Population after n years = P × (1 + r/100)^n
Value after n years of depreciation = P × (1 − r/100)^n

examples.question: A town has a population of 20,000. It grows by 10% annually. Find the population after two years.
A machine worth 100,000 depreciates by 10% each year. Find its value after two years.

sections.heading: 16. Election and Voting Problems
content: Election questions may include valid votes, invalid votes, votes not cast and winning margins.
Read carefully to identify whether a percentage is based on total voters, votes cast or valid votes.

examples.question: In an election, 10% of 8,000 registered voters did not vote. Find the number of votes cast.
examples.solution: Votes not cast = 10% of 8,000 = 800. Votes cast = 8,000 − 800 = 7,200.

examples.question: A candidate receives 55% of 12,000 valid votes. Find the number of votes received.

sections.heading: 17. Product-Constant Shortcut
content: Some placement questions keep a total product constant.
Examples include price and consumption when total expenditure remains unchanged.
If price increases, consumption must decrease to maintain the same expenditure.
formulas: Required reduction when price rises by r% = [r / (100 + r)] × 100
Required increase when price falls by r% = [r / (100 − r)] × 100

examples.question: The price of an item increases by 25%. By what percentage should consumption be reduced to keep expenditure unchanged?
The price of an item decreases by 20%. By what percentage can consumption increase without changing expenditure?

quickShortcuts.title: x% of y shortcut
quickShortcuts.note: x% of y is equal to y% of x. Choose the easier calculation.

quickShortcuts.title: Assume 100
quickShortcuts.note: When only percentages are given and no actual value is provided, assuming the original quantity as 100 often simplifies the problem.

commonMistakes: Dividing percentage change by the new value instead of the original value.
Assuming that a 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease gives no change.
Treating 'A is 25% more than B' as the same as 'B is 25% less than A'.
Using total votes when the question specifies valid votes.
Forgetting to convert a percentage into a fraction before multiplication.
Calculating a percentage without identifying the correct base quantity.
revisionChecklist: I can convert fractions and decimals into percentages.
I can find a percentage of a number quickly.
I can find the original value from a percentage.
I can calculate percentage increase and decrease.
I understand more-than and less-than comparisons.
I can solve marks, salary and expenditure questions.
I can solve population and depreciation questions.
